title: PhantomFix: A fake bug to Sentry Seer gets a coding agent to run attacker code
content:
Overview
A vulnerability exists in Sentry Seer when the system is configured to automatically hand issues to a coding agent for remediation. Successful exploitation results in arbitrary code execution within the coding‑agent environment and access to connected source repositories. This vulnerability is tracked as CVE-2026-90999.
Description
Sentry is a software error‑monitoring and performance‑tracking platform used by developers to detect, diagnose, and understand issues in their applications. It collects telemetry such as exceptions, stack traces, logs, and performance data from applications. Built into Sentry, Seer acts as an automated debugging assistant that converts telemetry into actionable remediation steps and can hand off issues to an integrated coding agent to propose code fixes.
Because Sentry front-end projects commonly expose a public DSN (Data Source Name) to allow browsers to submit this telemetry, an attacker can craft and submit malicious events through this public endpoint. When Seer is enabled to automatically pass issues to a coding agent, these attacker-supplied events can traverse multiple trust boundaries. Ultimately, malicious event fields propagate through Seer’s analysis pipeline, transforming into untrusted instructions that the privileged coding agent may execute.
The vulnerable workflow is as follows:
* Sentry ingests attacker‑generated exception events submitted through the public DSN.
* Seer evaluates whether the event represents an issue eligible for automated remediation.
* Seer generates a root‑cause analysis that uses attacker-controlled event fields, including exception messages, stack traces, source context, and breadcrumbs.
* The generated analysis is embedded directly into the initial prompt provided to the coding agent.
* The coding agent interprets the fabricated analysis as a legitimate description of the victim’s codebase.
* During its investigation, the coding agent downloads and executes a package controlled by the attacker.
* The package executes within the coding‑agent environment prior to any human review of a pull request.
Impact
Successful exploitation may allow arbitrary code execution in the coding‑agent environment that processes the affected repository.
Solution
At the time of this writing, no vendor‑supplied patch information has been provided. Mitigations may include disabling automated remediation flows, restricting coding‑agent package installation, or disabling Seer handoff until a fix is available. Additional defensive filtering of telemetry content before Seer analysis may also reduce risk.
Acknowledgements
Thank you to Nikita Benkovich and Vitalii Valkov, agyn for reporting this vulnerability. This document was written by Bob Kemerer.

report.summary: A critical Sentry Seer vulnerability lets attackers use fake bug reports via public DSNs to inject prompts and execute code in automated coding-agent environments.
report.background: Modern observability platforms have moved from passive error tracking to AI-assisted remediation. Sentry, widely used for exception and performance telemetry, exposes public Data Source Names (DSNs) so browsers and clients can submit events. Its Seer assistant analyzes those events and can hand issues to an integrated coding agent that proposes fixes. That workflow assumes telemetry is trustworthy diagnostic data, not attacker-controlled input. As AI agents gain permission to read repositories, install packages, and run code, the trust boundary between public telemetry and privileged automation becomes security-critical. CVE-2026-90999 shows what happens when that boundary is crossed: a fake exception crafted through a public DSN can become a malicious prompt. At disclosure time no vendor patch was available, so defenders must consider disabling automatic remediation or restricting agent capabilities.
key_points: Attack path: An attacker submits a crafted exception through a public Sentry DSN. Seer analyzes it, generates a root-cause report containing attacker-controlled fields, and passes that report to a coding agent as if it were a legitimate codebase description.

Prompt injection becomes code execution: The coding agent follows the fabricated analysis and downloads or executes an attacker-controlled package in its environment, granting arbitrary code execution before any human reviews a pull request.

Connected repositories are at risk: Because the agent operates with repository access, exploitation can expose source code, secrets, tokens, and CI/CD credentials, and may enable malicious commits or supply-chain changes.

No patch yet: CVE-2026-90999 had no vendor-supplied fix at disclosure. Recommended mitigations include disabling Seer handoff or automated remediation, blocking package installation by agents, and filtering telemetry before analysis.

Architectural issue: The bug shows that AI agents treat issue text, stack traces, breadcrumbs, and source context as instructions. Public telemetry endpoints are untrusted input and need strict separation from privileged automation.
report.impact: This vulnerability matters because automated remediation is a fast-growing AI feature, and it combines untrusted public input with privileged code execution. For the AI industry, it validates prompt injection as a supply-chain risk: agents that read telemetry, browse repositories, and install packages must treat all external content as adversarial. For developers, enabling Seer handoff without guards could let a fake bug compromise private repositories, secrets, and build systems; teams should audit agent permissions and require human approval before package installs or code execution. For regular users, the immediate risk is indirect, such as breaches or tampered releases from affected projects, but it reinforces that AI convenience features can expand attack surfaces. Vendors will likely need provenance checks, sandboxing, and policy controls for agent actions, not just better prompts.
report.tools: Related tools to watch: Sentry and Seer for patches and mitigations; coding agents such as GitHub Copilot coding agent, Cursor, Devin, and open-source alternatives like OpenHands and SWE-agent; prompt-injection defenses like Rebuff, LLM Guard, and OWASP LLM Top 10 guidance; sandboxing tools including gVisor, Firecracker, and Docker with seccomp; dependency and package controls such as Sigstore, npm provenance, and GitHub Actions OIDC. Monitor CVE-2026-90999 and CERT/CC advisories for vendor updates.
